title_en: The Sword Roars in the West Wind
subtitle_en: A Chronicle of the Central Special Branch
title_zh: 剑吼西风：中央特科纪事
title_file_as: Sword Roars in the West Wind, The
rights: Translation © the translator. Original text © Ye Xiaoshen / Gold Wall Press.
source_ref: 剑吼西风：中央特科纪事 (Gold Wall Press, Beijing, 1st ed. 2021.6; ISBN 978-7-5155-2038-4)
description: After the collapse of the Great Revolution in 1927, the Chinese Communist Party moved its central organs back to a Shanghai swarming with police, concession detectives, gangsters and informers. To protect the Party's leadership, Zhou Enlai built and led its first professional intelligence and security service, the Central Special Branch. Over eight years its agents penetrated the enemy's innermost councils, ran the Party's first double agent, opened its first underground courier line, built its first wireless set and cipher, founded its first secret archive, and hunted down the traitors who threatened it all. Ye Xiaoshen's narrative history draws on the scholarship and the memoirs to tell that hidden war street by street. This annotated English edition supplies the historical, cultural and geographic context a Western reader needs, and marks where the sources disagree.
translator_note: This is an English translation of Jian Hou Xi Feng: Zhongyang Teke Jishi (剑吼西风：中央特科纪事, “The Sword Roars in the West Wind: A Chronicle of the Central Special Branch”) by Ye Xiaoshen, published by Gold Wall Press in 2021. The source was an image-only scan with no digital text layer; the text was recovered by optical character recognition and verified page by page against the scanned original.

The book is a work of narrative history about the Central Special Branch (Zhongyang Teke), the Chinese Communist Party's first intelligence and security service, active in Shanghai from 1927 to 1935. It is written from within the Party's own tradition and frankly celebrates its subjects; footnotes mark where its claims are corroborated, uncorroborated, or contradicted by the wider scholarship, and where the account is that of an interested witness. Chinese personal and place names are given in pinyin except where an older English form is long established (Chiang Kai-shek, the Avenue Joffre). Where the scan was damaged or a reading uncertain, the note says so; no bridging text has been invented.

A word on conventions. Chinese names are romanized in pinyin, except for a few forms long fixed in English (Chiang Kai-shek, Sun Yat-sen, the Kuomintang, Whampoa) and for the Western scholars the author cites, who keep their own spellings. Streets in the foreign concessions are given by their period names, French or English, with today's pinyin name in a gloss at first mention (Avenue Joffre; Route Voisin, today Fumin Road). Distances are kept in the Chinese li where the phrase is idiomatic, glossed once, and given in metric where the source gives a plain figure. Sums of money appear as the source gives them, in silver dollars or in yuan. Dates are written month-day-year throughout.

One thing the reader should know going in. The book speaks from inside the Party's own tradition: it says “our Party,” calls the Party's enemies “reactionaries” and “running dogs,” and salutes its subjects as heroes and martyrs. That voice is the author's, deliberately preserved; it is not the translator's, and it is not neutral historical narration. Where the celebration outruns the record, or where the account is that of an interested witness, a footnote says so.
source_note: Image-only PDF scan, 350 pages, no text layer. Front cover (painting, reused as the ebook cover), back cover with blurb and ISBN, title page, CIP page, a Song-dynasty ci epigraph (He Zhu, from which the title is drawn), a five-page authorial preface, and a five-page table of contents precede the body. Simplified Chinese, horizontal setting. The printed-to-PDF offset is a constant 15 (printed = pdf - 15) across the whole book, with no unpaginated plate inserts; the preface runs a separate roman-numeral sequence. No library seal; clean scan.
